entries.title: Masked anti-migrant protesters block UK's Dover terminal
entries.summary: Chanting "stop the boats" and wearing balaclavas, the demonstrators blocked traffic at the UK's busiest international ferry port.
entries.content:
September 5, 2026

Chanting "stop the boats" and wearing balaclavas, the demonstrators blocked traffic at the UK's busiest international ferry port.

Hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover on Saturday as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.

Video footage showed demonstrators in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.

This came despite the fact that crossing dropped 40% between January and August 2026 compared to the previous year. However, the perceived threat of migrant boats has become a rallying cry for the far-right Reform UK party.

Police said that they were "engaging" with protesters and that normal traffic had resumed at the port after several hours.

Government condemns 'travel disruption'

"The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused," said a spokesman for the government of Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Under Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer, migrant crossings have been greatly reduced in part due to closer cooperation with French authorities.

Dover is the UK's biggest international ferry port, handling some 15,000 passengers a day during the summer and welcoming more than a third of the UK's trade goods with the European Union.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
entries.summary: As Germany heads into three elections in September, rumors are circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged

September 5, 2026

As Germany heads into three elections in September, rumors are circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.

Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. In Saxony-Anhalt, where voters go to the ballot boxes on Sunday, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could make history in by winning an outright majority.

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization", could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections. But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.

DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.

Does postal voting manipulate election results?

Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.

This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok, X and Facebook.

Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.

DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.

The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau, where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.

Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria, a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.

There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.

But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.

The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.

"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."

Postal voting easy to manipulate?

Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.

"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14. 

This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire, for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control." 

DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.

Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.

That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.

In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.

DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.

DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.

A familiar claim beyond Germany

The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.

During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.

Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.

"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.

He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.

"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.

This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

entries.title: Russia to pause strikes against Kyiv amid Ukraine talks
entries.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow to revive Ukraine peace talks. The trip is the pair's first visit to Kyiv since US President Donald Trump's reelection.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russia to pause strikes against Kyiv amid Ukraine talks

Published September 5, 2026last updated September 5, 2026

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow to revive Ukraine peace talks. They are also scheduled to visit Kyiv on Sunday,

Russia will pause strikes against Kyiv for three days, the Kremlin said on Saturday, coinciding with peace negoatiations led by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmirty Peskov told state media.

It comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks.

"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.

Kushner, Witkoff arrive in Moscow

The US envoys Kushner and Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Saturday. They were met at the airport by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

Hours earlier, US President Donald Trump said he was sending his son-in-law Kushner and businessman Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv with a proposal to end the conflict.

"They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war," Trump told reporters Friday when asked about the pair's trip. Kushner and Witkoff have served as Trump's envoys to lead peace efforts in the Middle East as well as Ukraine.

The US president did not provide any details on the potential plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."

US envoys to visit Kyiv next

Zelenskyy announced earlier on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.

Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.

Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting. 

Drone strikes continue

Meanwhile, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service (SBU) in Kyiv on Friday.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike "a major escalation" of the war.

"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he wrote on X.

Zelenskyy said he ordered "an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."

Ukraine has also launched repeated drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and the retail giant Wildberries. 

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru, Wesley Dockery, Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Iran war: Explosions reported near Kharg Island
entries.summary: Iranian media has reported that a tanker was targeted near the oil hub of Kharg Island. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: Explosions reported near Kharg Island

Published September 5, 2026last updated September 5, 2026

Iranian media has reported that a tanker was targeted near the oil hub of Kharg Island. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Below is a roundup of the top headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the wider Middle East region on Saturday, September 5.

  • Explosions near Kharg Island, Iranian media reports
  • US and Iranian officials have not officially commented on the reports
  • US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee visits West Bank village home to Palestinian-Americans amid rise of settler attacks

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Huckabee claims no Gaza displacement is planned

Huckabee claims no Gaza displacement is planned

US Ambassador Mike Huckabee said on a visit with Palestinian-Americans on the West Bank that Israel had no plans to forcibly displace people from Gaza just two days after the government laid out a plan to do so.

"I can tell you categorially there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will," Huckabee told journalists.

However, on Thursday, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir announced his proposal to have 250,000 Palestinians leave Gaza in the first year of his plan, followed by the rest of two million some residents over the next six years.

A day earlier, Defense Minister Israel Katz had said that the Israeli government was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza, but was waiting for discussions with the United States over where displaced people should go.

Skip next section Israel, Hezbollah flare-up in southern Lebanon

Israel, Hezbollah flare-up in southern Lebanon

Despite a ceasefire that went into effect over two months ago, flare-ups are continuing between Israel and Hezbollah over one strategic hill in southern Lebanon.

Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah, a Shiite political party and paramilitary group supported by Iran, intensified once again earlier this year in the wider context of the US-Iran war. The US, Germany and several Arab countries consider Hezbollah a terrorist organization, whereas the EU only deems Hezbollah's armed wing a terror group.

While the fiercest battles are over, the two sides are still in conflict over the Ali Taher hill, which overlooks the city of Nabatiyeh. According to the Lebanese Health Ministry, at least five people have died and 24 have been injured in the fighting since Friday.

The United States, which has mediated peace talks, has wanted Hezbollah to hand the hill over the Lebanese government, but the militant group has refused to withdraw from certain positions north of the Litani river where Ali Taher sits.

There are fears that the fighting could escalate into an all-out battle for Nabatiyeh and lead to more violence across Lebanon, complicating efforts to resolve the war in Iran.

Skip next section US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee in West Bank

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee in West Bank

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee was in the occupied West Bank on Saturday to meet with Palestinian-Americans who have faced violent attacks from Israeli settlers in recent months.

"Our clear message is that crime is crime, terror is terror. When people do it they should have an expectation that they will have severe consequences," Huckabee told reporters from the town of Turmus Ayya. He declined to directly criticize Israeli policy but said that Israel "has responsibility" to protect West Bank Palestinians.

This year has seen a significant uptick in Israeli settlers attacking Palestinian homes in the West Bank, including shootings and arson attacks.

Skip next section Explosions heard near Iran's Kharg Island, reports say

Explosions heard near Iran's Kharg Island, reports say

Official Iranian news agencies reported a strike near the fuel hub of Kharg Island that appeared to target an oil tanker.

However, they also reported that no smoke could be seen rising from the area.

Neither the US nor the Iranian government have commented on the strikes

After a lull in fighting, the US began striking Iranian targets again last Sunday. The war has now entered its seventh month.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

As the US risks sliding into another "forever war," Iranian broadcasters have reported strikes of unknown origin on Kharg Island.

Meanwhile, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is due to visit Palestinian-Americans in West Bank towns that have come under Israeli settler attacks.

entries.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
entries.summary: Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.
entries.content:
September 5, 2026

Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven. "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Migration: A burden or an asset?

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

Who's welcome – and who isn't?

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Why many Syrians feel Assad's death sentence isn't enough
entries.summary: In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to transitional justice.
entries.content:
September 5, 2026

In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to transitional justice.

Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad. 

Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.

Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.

"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."

Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.

Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."

Justice served in Syria?

The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."

Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.

In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.

Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.

But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.

Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.

Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.

In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.

Victim-centered process needed

Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."

For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.

Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.

For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.

"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."

At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.

"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."

Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.

"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."

The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.

The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".

Investigating all war crimes

"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."

For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.

"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.

Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.

It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.

In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.

"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."

This article was originally written in German.

Skip next section Traffic rehearsals, steep hotel prices as New Delhi gears up for BRICS

Traffic rehearsals, steep hotel prices as New Delhi gears up for BRICS

In a week from now, leaders and representatives of BRICS nations will descend upon New Delhi to attend the 18th summit of the international group which India is hosting as part of its 2026 presidency.

The summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital.

Preparations are entering their final stage ahead of the meet and Delhi is set to be a fortress with a heavy security blanket.

On Saturday, a motorcade rehearsal had been scheduled with the traffic authorities in Delhi issuing an advisory for diversions and regulated movement on key routes.

The Indian Express has reported that drones would be deployed to track the movement of traffic and spot chokepoints during the summit.

Meanwhile, media reports earlier this week said that hotel prices in the capital were soaring around the dates of the summit.

Indian news outlets said that luxury hotels in the city were either fully sold out or were giving rooms at a significantly higher tariff.

For one luxury hotel in central Delhi, a room that costs 23,000 Indian Rupees (€210, $243 approx) a night this weekend was listed at 280,000 Indian Rupees (€2,550, $2,963 approx) per night from September 10 to 13, with the rates going back to normal from September 14th, a search on a travel app showed.

India's fourth round of BRICS chairship

BRICS is an 11-member bloc which brings together major emerging markets and developing countries of the world. 

India said the upcoming meet will also be joined by partner countries and outreach invitees.

The group's presidency rotates annually among the member states.

India, which is also a founding member of BRICS, has previously held the presidency thrice — in 2012, 2016 and 2021.

India's BRICS chairship is guided by the theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," according to a statement by the foreign ministry in New Delhi.

Skip next section Indian athletes prepare for Asian Games by spending night in shipping container-like units

Indian athletes prepare for Asian Games by spending night in shipping container-like units

India's athletes are gearing up for this month's Asian Games being hosted by Japan and their preparations involve living temporarily in shipping container-style units to acclimate to their official lodgings during the continental sporting event. 

The Japanese prefecture of Aichi will stage the Games from September 19 to October 4, with over 17,000 athletes and ​officials in attendance.

The number of participants is higher than the Olympics and in a cost-cutting move, they will not stay in a traditional athletes' village but in hotels, a cruise ship and temporary units mostly made of wood.

The Sports Authority of India (SAI) has constructed similar wooden container-style accommodations at its athlete headquarters in Patiala and Bengaluru to replicate the arrangement in Japan.

In the SAI's southern Indian campus in Bengaluru, two fully air-conditioned container-style units have been built, measuring 40-foot-long (12 meters) ​and 10-foot-wide.

Each unit two small twin bedrooms, two bathrooms, a ​kitchen and ⁠a living area with a TV and music ⁠system.

Up north in Punjab's Patiala, SAI gave journalists a tour of the two cabins built there.

"These containers are like a simulator," Vineet Kumar, deputy director general of the SAI, told news agency AFP in Patiala.

"It is a unique concept as never in an Asian Games or Olympics this kind of accommodation was used," he said.

Kumar told AFP that the replicas were made to ensure that Indian athletes "don't feel the shock and get claustrophobic when they are given such accommodation in Japan."

The SAI told the media that a roster has been made for the athletes to stay for a night, turn-by-turn, before they fly out for Japan.

Skip next section India marks Teachers' Day

India marks Teachers' Day

India is celebrating its national Teachers' Day on Saturday.

Every year on September 5, educational institutions across the country hold cultural events and programs honoring teachers for their contributions to the society.

Teachers' Day in India is celebrated on the birth anniversary of renowned scholar and philosopher Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan who was born on September 5, 1888 and served as the second president of the nation.

The commemoration dates back to 1962, a few months after he became president.

According to a popular anecdote, some of Radhakrishnan's students wanted to celebrate his birthday but the academic-turned-statesman is believed to have told them that it would be his "proud privilege" if the day was observed as Teachers' Day instead.

On Saturday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended Teachers’ Day greetings.

"#TeachersDay is about appreciating the strong contribution of teachers to our society. It is also a day to pay homage to Dr. S. Radhakrishnan," he wrote on X as he shared visuals of his meeting with the recipients of the annual National Teachers' Awards that were presented on Friday.

Skip next section Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275

Nepal floods: India says tally of missing Indians at 275

India has said that 275 of its nationals remain missing, ten days after flash floods ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border.

A total of 169 Indians have been rescued so far from the flood-affected areas in Nepal, India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Friday evening. 

Jaiswal said that in the latest rescue three Indians, including a five-year-old, were pulled to safety from Trishuli Bazaar in Nepal.

"Our Embassy in Nepal is assisting in their return to India by air," he said on X.

The spokesperson told a press conference in New Delhi that 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.

No Indian travelers are now stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region, Jaiswal announced, citing official Chinese sources.

Nepal's official death toll from the deluge now stands at 1,294, with 5,053 still missing.

A frantic rescue effort has gone on for days to search for survivors, especially at mud-filled hydropower tunnels, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.

Indian team assists in Rasuwa tunnel rescue

On Saturday, New Delhi's envoy to Kathmandu said that an Indian tunnel rescue team, working with Nepal's defense forces at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, had stepped up operations.

"The Indian tunnel rescue team working alongside with Nepali Army dug deeper into Chilime tunnel yesterday draining out water. A temporary track is also being made to allow more heavy equipment to reach tunnel," Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava said.

He added that doctors accompanying the Indian rescuers had also held a health camp for the local community.

India has also supplied nearly 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the floods hit the country on August 26, Jaiswal said on Friday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi from DW's studio in Delhi, bringing you the weekend edition of our India blog where we break down all the biggest headlines that are making a splash in the world's most populous nation. 

A total of 275 Indians are still missing in the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods as deaths in the disaster cross the 1,200 mark.

In diplomatic news, a countdown has begun in New Delhi for next week's BRICS summit. India is set to host leaders of member nations as the economic bloc's chair.

Meanwhile in the world of sports, Indian athletes are prepping for the Asian Games in a rather unconventional manner — by sleeping in shipping container-style units.

Stay tuned for all this and more.

entries.title: Germany news: Thousands expected at Saxony-Anhalt rallies
entries.summary: Ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday, a democracy festival by civil society groups is planned in Magdeburg. The far-right AfD will also hold its final campaign rally in the state capital. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Thousands expected at Saxony-Anhalt rallies

Published September 5, 2026last updated September 5, 2026

Ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday, a democracy festival by civil society groups is planned in Magdeburg. The far-right AfD will also hold its final campaign rally in the state capital. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police say 12 rallies are planned ahead of Sunday's election in Saxony-Anhalt
  • Rhine states seek additional funding after low-water crisis
  • Police hunt possible 'climate extremist' after power grid sabotage
  • Hackers carry out threat to release Berlin state records

Here is our roundup of news and analysis from Germany on Saturday, September 5

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Steinmeier urges unity ahead of Saxony-Anhalt election

Steinmeier urges unity ahead of Saxony-Anhalt election

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned that Germany's democracy and rule of law need protection from those "who scorn and trample all over them."

Steinmeier was speaking ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to receive by far the most votes.

While not singling out any party, he appeared to take aim at AfD's policies and rhetoric, which critics describe as extremist and anti-migrant and supporters label a patriotic defense of national borders and security.

"Ethnic-based thinking and nationalist isolationism are simply not the answer to the challenges of the 21st century," Steinmeier told a community festival in Bonn.

Steinmeier, who steps down from office in March after ten years, described liberal democracy as an "achievement" and "a blessing for us all."

He said those who wish to protect and preserve democracy represent the majority and that anger and outrage offer no way forward.

"You cannot build a future on hatred and incitement," Steinmeier warned.

Skip next section Manhunt continues after sabotage on German power grid

Manhunt continues after sabotage on German power grid

Police in Germany continue to hunt for a 48-year-old man suspected of causing deliberate damage to the country's electricity grid.

The most serious incident was on Tuesday evening at a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne.

Launch devices were used to fire cables across overhead lines, causing a short circuit that forced five units of the nearby Niederaussem coal plant to temporarily disconnect from the network.

Earlier the same day, a similar attack was carried out near the Jänschwalde plant in eastern Brandenburg. More than a dozen launch devices were found.

On Thursday, a passer-by found similar unused devices at a substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf.

Police say the objects matched the launch gear used in the other incidents.

Germany's DPA news agency reported on Friday that a man from a town near Dortmund claimed responsibility for the incidents in two letters.

His motive is reportedly to draw attention to the use of fossil fuels in electricity production, which he called a "crime."

This week, officers found explosives in the 48-year-old's home, while a special operations unit stormed a truck in a wood, some 100 kilometers (62 miles) away. The suspect was not found.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the acts as "climate extremism."

Skip next section FBI puts German fraudster on Most Wanted list

FBI puts German fraudster on Most Wanted list

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has added German national Bernhard Fritsch to its Most Wanted Fraudsters list.

Fritsch was convicted by a jury in Los Angeles last year of fleecing investors of about $26.8 million (€23.1 million) with a fake celebrity-influencer app.

Instead of building the product, prosecutors say the 65-year-old spent millions on cars, a yacht and a Malibu villa.

Fritsch was sentenced to 15 years in prison in absentia after fleeing to Mexico.

Despite being detained by immigration officials in Mexico, he then fled to Germany and is believed to be in the Munich area.

The FBI is prepared to pay up to $150,000 for any information about his whereabouts.

Skip next section Four states demand federal support to waterways after drought

Four states demand federal support to waterways after drought

After a summer drought caused severe low water levels on the Rhine River, four of Germany's states have called on Berlin to increase funding to modernize inland waterways.

Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia said the federal government must invest at least €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) per year to boost maintenance.

Germany's waterways, including the Rhine, play a key role in moving raw materials across the country, carrying more than 5% of all freight transported,

They said politicians often focus on investing in roads and railways, while canals and rivers often get neglected.

Over the summer, the Rhine became almost impassable at one key location and many ships plying the Rhine had to operate with much-reduced cargoes.

Economists at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated the drought would cause an economic loss of up to €2 billion.

North Rhine-Westphalia's Transport Minister Viktor Haase called for new fleets of inland vessels that can reliably operate even in extreme low-water conditions.

Skip next section Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election

Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election

Thousands of people are expected at rallies in eastern Germany's state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of elections for a new regional parliament.

Police said 12 events have been registered in the state capital, Magdeburg, with others in Halle.

Most of the demonstrations are against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which is widely expected to receive the most support in Sunday's vote.

Trade unions and civil society groups are organizing the largest rallies. Their events include a so-called democracy festival.

The AfD will also hold its final campaign event in Magdeburg.

The latest polls put the AfD at over 40% support, putting it on course to be the largest party in the state parliament by a wide margin.

However, without an outright majority, the chance of the AfD forming a government will get messy as mainstream parties have ruled out a coalition with the far right.

No smaller party expected to enter parliament has offered to formally support an AfD-led government.

The AfD could take office on its own only if it wins a majority of seats.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from Germany, where more than a dozen rallies are planned ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

For the first time since World War II, a far-right party — the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — could win the most votes and could theoretically take power in the eastern German state.

After cargo shipping was disrupted due to severe low water levels on the Rhine River this summer, four German states have asked the federal government for additional support.

Also, the FBI has added a German businessman from Bavaria to its most-wanted list.

entries.title: What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
entries.summary: Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to drastically overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does the party have planned?
entries.content:
Germany

What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?

September 5, 2026

Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to drastically overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does the party have planned?

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.

The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."

Radical tightening of asylum laws

In its draft government program, the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.

The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."

Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.

Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.

And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.

Anti-immigration policy

The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.

However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.

To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."

Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.

Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.

"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."

Rapprochement with Russia

The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.

For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.

The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.

The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.

On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.

Establishing citizen patrols

Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."

Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.

A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.

Radical change in social policy

A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.

It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy." 

To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Tunisia: Judge orders arrest of journalist Mohamed Yousfi
entries.summary: A journalist and vocal critic of the Tunisian president, Mohamed Yousfi has been taken into custody ahead of an interview. A union called the arrest an attack on all journalists' rights.
entries.content:
September 5, 2026

A journalist and vocal critic of the Tunisian president, Mohamed Yousfi has been taken into custody ahead of an interview. A union called the arrest an attack on all journalists' rights.

A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT.

Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM, but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities.

The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source.

No reason provided for detention

Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.

Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention.

"He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post.

The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia, where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution.

Attack on freedom of the press

SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media.

Rights ⁠groups ​warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent ​voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia.

In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power. 

Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in ​absentia.

On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports.

The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
